Fragmenta in epistulam ad Kolossenses (in catenis)
314 Τὰ πολλὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς ταύτης δυσχερῆ ἔχει τὴν κατανόησιν διὰ τὸ πολλοὺς μὴ
γινώσκειν τὴν ὑπό315 θεσιν τοῦ γράμματος καὶ τὸν σκοπὸν τοῦ ἀποστόλου. ἡ δὲ
ὑπόθεσίς ἐστιν αὕτη. Οἱ ἀπὸ Ἑλλήνων πιστεύσαντες εἶχον τοὺς ἔτι Ἕλληνας
ἀφέλκοντας αὐτοὺς εἰς τὰς παρατηρήσεις τὰς Ἑλληνικάς, οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων τοὺς
Ἰουδαίους παρακελεύοντας τὸν νόμον τηρεῖν, ὡς τῆς χάριτος ἀτελεστέρας οὔσης
ἄνευ τοῦ νόμου. ὁ δὲ λόγος ἦν τοῖς Ἕλλησι πρὸς αὐτοὺς ὅτι δίκαιον καὶ ἀγγέλοις
προσκυνεῖν, τοὺς θεοὺς αὐτῶν ἀγγέλους λέγοντες εἶναι· τὸν γὰρ θεὸν μέγαν ὄντα
καὶ ἀνθρώποις ἀνέφικτον, διὰ τῶν ἀγγέλων τούτων ὥσπερ μεσιτῶν χορηγεῖν τὰς
ἐνεργείας τοῖς δεομένοις. ἴσασι δέ, φασί, καὶ αἱ γραφαὶ τὴν τῶν ἀγγέλων ὠφέλειαν·
καὶ γὰρ ὁ θεὸς ἔστησεν ὅρια ἐθνῶν κατ' ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων θεοῦ, καὶ Μιχαὴλ ἄρχων
τῶν Ἰουδαίων, καὶ ὁ ἄρχων τῆς Περσίδος ἕτερος ἄγγελος. καὶ πάλιν· ἰδοὺ ὁ ἄρχων
τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἔρχεται, καὶ Ἰακώβ· ὁ ἄγγελος ὁ ῥυόμενός με, καὶ ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι περὶ
τοῦ ἀποστόλου Πέτρου· ὁ ἄγγελος αὐτοῦ, φασίν, ἔστιν, καὶ ὁ κύριος περὶ τῶν
παιδίων· μὴ κωλύετε αὐτὰ ἔρχεσθαι πρός με, ὅτι οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτῶν διὰ παντὸς
βλέ316 πουσι τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ πατρός μου τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς. ἀπὸ γὰρ τούτων
ἁπάντων ὧν οἱ μὲν ἐπίστευον οἱ δὲ ἠπίστουν, συνήγοντο καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ Ἕλληνες,
φάσκοντες περιττὴν εἶναι τὴν διὰ τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ χάριν ἀρκούντων τῶν ἀγγέλων
τῶν ἀπ' αἰῶνος τοὺς πειθομένους προσάγειν τῷ θεῷ ἀτελὲς δὲ ἔλεγον πάσας τὰς
παρατηρήσεις παρορᾶν τὰς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις καὶ Ἕλλησιν πρὸς ταῦτα ὁ σκοπὸς τῶν
ἀποστόλων τῆς ἐν χερσὶν ἐπιστολῆς. 314,col2 Ἄξιον δὲ τὴν ὑπόθεσιν εἰπεῖν ἣν ἐκ
τῆς ἐπιστολῆς εὕρομεν· ἑτέρως γὰρ παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς 315,col2 νοεῖται πολλὰ τῆς
πρὸς Kolοσσαεῖς διὰ τὸ τὴν ὑπόθεσιν μὴ πάνυ γινώσκεσθαι μηδὲ τὸν σκοπὸν τοῦ
ἀποστόλου. Οἱ ἀπὸ Ἑλλήνων πιστεύσαντες εἶχον καὶ τοὺς ἔτι Ἕλληνας ἀνθέλκειν
εἰς τὰς παρατηρήσεις τὰς Ἑλληνικὰς βουλομένους, καὶ τῶν Ἰουδαίων τοὺς
πιστεύσαντας πείθοντας τὸν νόμον τηρεῖν, ὡς τῆς χάριτος ἀτελεστέρας οὔσης ἄνευ
τοῦ νόμου. πρὸς τούτοις καὶ Ἕλληνες καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι τοὺς Kolοσσαέας ἔπειθον
ἀγγέλοις προσέχειν· Ἕλληνες μὲν τοὺς θεοὺς αὐτῶν λέγοντες ἀγγέλους εἶναι, ὅτι τε
ὁ μὲν θεὸς ἀχώρητος καὶ μέγας, οὐκ ἐφικτὸς ἀνθρώποις, διὰ δὲ τῶν ἀγγέλων τούτων
ὥσπερ μεσιτῶν χορηγεῖ τὰς εὐεργεσίας τοῖς δεχομένοις· οἱ δὲ Ἰουδαῖοι, ὅτι ὁ θεὸς
ἔστησεν ὅρια ἐθνῶν κατ' ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων θεοῦ· οὕτω καὶ Μιχαὴλ ἄρχων τῶν
Ἰουδαίων, οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἄρχων Περσίδος ἀντέστη μοι. καὶ πάλιν· ἰδοὺ ὁ ἄρχων τῶν
Ἑλλήνων ἤρχετο, ὡς καὶ ὁ Ἰακώβ· ὁ ἄγγελος ὁ ῥυόμενός με ἐκ νεότητός μου, καὶ ἐν
ταῖς καθόλου Πράξεσι περὶ Πέτρου· ἄγγελος αὐτοῦ ἐστιν, καὶ ὁ κύριος· ὁρᾶτε μὴ
καταφρονήσητε ἑνὸς τῶν μικρῶν τούτων, ὅτι οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτῶν τὸ πρόσωπον
316,col2 ὁρῶσι τοῦ πατρός μου τοῦ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς. ἀπὸ γὰρ τούτων ἁπάντων ὧν
τοῖς μὲν ἐπίστευον τοῖς δὲ ἠπίστουν, συνῆγον καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ Ἕλληνες τὸ περιττὴν
εἶναι τὴν διὰ τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ χάριν ὄντων ἀγγέλων τῶν ἀπ' αἰῶνος τοὺς
πειθομένους προσαγόντων. ἀτελὲς δὲ καὶ τὸ τὰς παρατηρήσεις παρορᾶν τάς τε παρ'
Ἕλλησι καὶ παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις. πρὸς ταῦτα ὁ σκοπὸς τῷ Παύλῳ, καὶ ταῦτα διορθοῦται.
διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἀρχόμενός φησίν· Kol 1,2 Ἐπισημήνασθαι χρὴ διότι ἐν ὀλίγοις στίχοις
πολλάκις τοῦ Χριστοῦ μέμνηται· τοῦ γὰρ ἀθετουμένου συνεχῶς ποιεῖται τὴν μνήμην
ἐντυπῶν ταῖς ψυχαῖς τὸν εἰς αὐτὸν πόθον. Kol 1,5–6 Ἤδη αὐτοὺς ὑποδείκνυσιν, ὅτι
τὴν ἐλπίδα τὴν ἀποκειμένην τῆς ἀναστάσεως καὶ τῆς βασιλείας οὐκ ἀγγέλων
διοίκησις κατώρθωσεν, ἀλλ' ἡ παρουσία τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. ∆ιὰ τοῦ
εἰπεῖν τῷ λόγῳ τῆς ἀληθείας δείκνυσιν ὡς οὐκ ἀκίνδυνον παροφθῆναι τὸ

[Edition heading: Fragments on the letter to the Colossians (in the catenas).]
[First catena form, argument of the letter:] Many things of this letter have a difficult understanding because many do not know the subject of the letter and the aim of the apostle. And the subject is this. Those who believed from the Greeks had the still-Greeks dragging them off to the Greek observances; and those from the Jews had the Jews urging them to keep the law, as though grace were less complete without the law. And the argument of the Greeks to them was that it is right to worship angels too, saying that their gods are angels; for God, being great and unreachable for human beings, supplies his workings to those in need through these angels as through mediators. And the Scriptures too, they say, know the help of the angels: for God set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and Michael is ruler of the Jews; and the ruler of Persia is another angel; and again, "Behold, the ruler of the Greeks is coming"; and Jacob: "the angel who delivers me"; and in the Acts about the apostle Peter: "it is his angel," they say; and the Lord about the children: "Do not hinder them from coming to me, for their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." For from all these, of whom some believed and some disbelieved, both Jews and Greeks drew together, declaring the grace through the Lord Jesus superfluous, since the angels from of old suffice to bring to God those who obey; and they said it was incomplete to overlook all the observances among Jews and Greeks. Against these things is the aim of the apostles of the letter in hand.
[Second catena form, edition pages 314-316, column 2:] It is worth stating the subject which we found from the letter; for many things of the letter to the Colossians are understood otherwise by most people, because the subject is not well known, nor the aim of the apostle. Those who believed from the Greeks had the still-Greeks wanting to drag them back to the Greek observances, and those of the Jews who believed had (Jews) persuading them to keep the law, as though grace were less complete without the law. Besides these, both Greeks and Jews were persuading the Colossians to give heed to angels: the Greeks saying that their gods are angels, and that God is uncontainable and great, not reachable by human beings, but through these angels as mediators supplies his benefits to those who receive them; the Jews, that God set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; so also Michael is ruler of the Jews, so also "the ruler of Persia withstood me"; and again, "behold, the ruler of the Greeks was coming"; as also Jacob: "the angel who delivers me from my youth"; and in the general Acts about Peter: "it is his angel"; and the Lord: "See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels see the face of my Father who is in the heavens." For from all these, some of which they believed and some they disbelieved, both Jews and Greeks concluded that the grace through the Lord Jesus Christ is superfluous, since there are angels from of old bringing near those who obey; and that it is incomplete to overlook the observances both among Greeks and among Jews. Against these is Paul's aim, and he corrects these things. For this reason, as he begins, he says:
Colossians 1:2. One must note that in a few lines he mentions Christ many times; for he constantly makes mention of the one being set aside, imprinting on their souls the longing for him.
Colossians 1:5-6. Already he points out to them that the hope laid up, of the resurrection and of the kingdom, the administration of angels did not accomplish, but the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ. By saying "in the word of the truth" he shows that it is not without danger for the [continues in the next section: gospel] to be overlooked
pass_b_english: Much of this letter is hard to understand, because many people do not know what occasioned it or what the apostle was aiming at. The occasion was this. Believers who had come from among the Greeks had Greeks who were still pagans pulling them back to Greek observances. Believers from among the Jews had Jews urging them to keep the law, as though grace without the law were less than complete. The Greeks’ argument to them was that it is right to worship angels as well, for they said their gods were angels: God is great and out of human reach, and so he supplies his workings to those in need through these angels, as through go-betweens. And the Scriptures too, they said, know how angels help us: God “set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deuteronomy 32:8); Michael is the ruler of the Jews (Daniel 10:21); the ruler of Persia is another angel (Daniel 10:13); and again, “Behold, the ruler of the Greeks is coming” (Daniel 10:20). Jacob says, “the angel who delivers me” (Genesis 48:16). In the Acts, about the apostle Peter, they say, “It is his angel” (Acts 12:15). And the Lord said about the children, “Do not stop them from coming to me” (Matthew 19:14), “for their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). From all these texts Jews and Greeks alike, some of them believers and some not, drew their conclusion: the grace that comes through the Lord Jesus is superfluous, since the angels, who have been there from the beginning, are enough to bring to God those who obey; and to neglect all the observances kept by Jews and Greeks, they said, was to fall short of perfection. The apostles’ aim in the letter before us is directed against all this.

The second catena form adds: It is worth setting out the occasion of the letter as we have found it from the letter itself. … God is uncontainable … The Jews argued that God set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; that Michael is ruler of the Jews; that “the ruler of Persia withstood me” (Daniel 10:13); and “the angel who delivers me from my youth” … And the Lord said, “See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). … This is what Paul is aiming at, and he sets these things right. That is why he says at the very beginning:
On Colossians 1:2: Notice that in a few lines he names Christ many times. Christ was the one they were setting aside, so Paul keeps mentioning him, to stamp on their souls a longing for him.

On Colossians 1:5–6: He is already showing them that the hope laid up for us, the hope of the resurrection and of the kingdom, was not won by the administration of angels but by the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ. choices.term: 314,col2 Ἄξιον δὲ τὴν ὑπόθεσιν εἰπεῖν … διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἀρχόμενός φησίν·
choices.english: Doublet collapsed: first catena form kept in full; second form reduced to 'The second catena form adds:' with only its material that has no counterpart in the first
choices.why: The edition prints the argument of the letter in two parallel catena forms (the second marked 314,col2-316,col2). Kept from the second: finding the argument from the letter, 'uncontainable', the attribution of the Scripture proofs to the Jews, 'withstood me', 'from my youth', the Matthew 18:10 wording 'see that you do not despise one of these little ones', and the closing sentence that leads into the 1:2 note.

choices.english: That is why he says at the very beginning: / On Colossians 1:2:
choices.why: The old English printed a stray 'beginning (Col 1:2)'; ἀρχόμενος is 'as he begins'.

choices.term: ὁ ἄγγελος ὁ ῥυόμενός με ἐκ νεότητός μου
choices.english: “the angel who delivers me from my youth”, uncited
choices.why: The second form joins Genesis 48:16 ('the angel who delivers me') with 'from my youth' from 48:15 (LXX 'who fed me from my youth'); the first form's shorter quotation carries the Genesis 48:16 reference.

choices.term: μὴ κωλύετε αὐτὰ ἔρχεσθαι πρός με, ὅτι οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτῶν …
choices.english: “Do not stop them from coming to me” (Matthew 19:14), “for their angels always see …” (Matthew 18:10)
choices.why: The first form runs two Gospel sayings together; each half is cited to its own verse.

choices.term: ὁ θεὸς ἔστησεν ὅρια ἐθνῶν κατ' ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων θεοῦ
choices.why: Septuagint wording of Deuteronomy 32:8 (Hebrew/KJV: 'children of Israel'); same verse.
The sentence runs on into u01-rem-early; ellipsis at the break.
The first form has the plural; kept as written (the second form has 'Paul').
